newsitem.title: USA: IPO VIEW - Buying opportunities seen in aftermarket.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Buying opportunities seen in aftermarket.

text.p: As the initial public offering market flounders and many new issues trade at a discount, the time may be right to snap up stocks at a bargain in the aftermarket.

"Some of the IPOs that will be priced between now and summer will probably lose between 15 percent and 30 percent from the offer price," said Manish Shah of the IPO Maven. "This is precisely the time that investors should be focusing more and more on the aftermarket than at the IPO level."
According to research firm Securities Data Co., of 136 IPOs priced this year, 55 were trading below their offer price as of March 26.

"They (small investors) may not have the opportunity to buy on the IPO but certainly could benefit from the weaker market in the aftermarket," said Barbara Bradley, managing director of syndicate at Laidlaw Equities.
She said that significant buying opportunities existed as long as the fundamentals of the deal were examined carefully, and the investor was willing to have some patience.

In the short term, however, the incentives to tap into the IPO market have not been overwhelming. Securities Data estimates that average gains on IPOs this year from the offer date through to March 26 came in at a lowly 1.3 percent. CommScan, a New York-based research firm, puts this number at 1.71 percent.

Some market watchers cited the skittishness of stock markets as a reason to stay away from new issues. "There are going to be compelling valuations but what are you buying in the face of?" questioned Linda Intini, vice president of Citibank Global Asset Management.
She said she would recommend staying on the IPO sidelines till there was more confidence in the stock markets.

A renewal of confidence required good corporate earnings, analysts said. Disappointing earnings amid a rising interest rate environment would translate into a "volatile, if not downward-trending market," said Intini.
This would bode ill for IPOs, which needed, she said, "a good stock environment like we've had in '95 and '96...when investors were willing to take risks."
And so the IPO market may have to wait a while before it sees a resurgence of interest. Activity was quiet last week, and more than a few debuts were made on the back of price cuts.

Hamilton Bancorp Inc. was an exception, opening with a 1-1/4 point premium after coming to market towards the upper end of its filing range, and holding on to the gains despite Thursday's sharp fall in stocks.
On Thursday, the Dow Jones industrial average closed down 140.11 points, or 2.04 percent, at 6,740.59. U.S. financial markets were closed Friday.

For this week, some issues could "do reasonably well by recent standards," said John Fitzgibbon of the IPO Aftermarket. Triton Systems Inc.'s offering, which has been pushed back a number of times, is slated for this week and could fetch a premium of 3/4 to one point, he said.
Auto-By-Tel Corp.'s $40 million deal could also see an opening pop, as could AmeriPath Inc.'s, offering of 6.2 million shares with an expected price range of $13 to $15 a share.
Other deals that Fitzgibbon said may garner premiums include ASI Solutions Inc. and Gulf Island Fabrication Inc.
